title: Document Management System
tagline: A tool that reads old scanned records and suggests how to file them, with a person approving each one
summary: At my 2026 internship, the county was scanning about 300,000 pages of traffic signal records, some going back to 1972. After scanning, someone still had to open every PDF, figure out what it was, find the date and signal number, rename it and log it in a spreadsheet. I built a prototype that does the reading first and hands a person a suggestion to approve.

overview.what: A prototype that reads old scanned traffic signal records, figures out what each one is, and suggests a file name and details for a person to approve.
overview.why: The county was scanning about 300,000 pages of records, some from 1972. After scanning, someone still had to open every PDF, work out what it was, rename it and log it by hand.
overview.did: I built it at my 2026 internship at GPI: text reading for old scans, three separate ways of guessing each document's type, a review screen that shows where every suggestion came from, and accounts for helpers and experts.
overview.result: When it was confident, it matched the county's own category about 97% of the time, and it got the type right on all 26 documents in a blind test. Dates and exact names were harder, so a person still checks every one.

hero.caption: Scans waiting for a person to review.

sections.heading: Seeing the bottleneck
body: The records filled about 50 filing cabinets: signal plans, timing sheets, work orders and more. One team was scanning everything into PDFs, and I could see the next step turning into another huge manual job. So I started building something before the process was even settled.

media.alt: Two workflow diagrams comparing the former five-step manual document process with the four-step evidence-backed review process
media.caption: The old five-step routine next to the new review flow.

sections.heading: The software suggests, a person decides
body: The main rule was that it never files anything on its own. For every value it suggests, it remembers exactly where on the page it found it, so you can click a suggestion and jump straight to that spot on the scan. If it can't read a handwritten date, it says so and you type it in.

media.alt: Document review workspace showing extracted fields, classifier votes, OCR text, and the scanned document side by side
media.caption: Suggested fields, the evidence for them, and the scan, all on one screen.

sections.heading: Reading 50-year-old paper
body: Getting text out of old scans was its own challenge. I used two OCR tools: one for normal typed pages, and another for big plan drawings, where I zoomed in on the corners because that's where the title blocks usually are. Handwriting was still the weak spot.

To figure out what kind of document each scan was, I used three separate methods: key phrases that only show up on one kind of form, a comparison against about 140 documents the county had already filed, and a small local AI. When they agree, it's confident. When they don't, it waits for a person.

media.alt: Flowchart showing scanned files moving through OCR, three independent classification methods, confidence fusion, metadata extraction, human review, and approved filing
media.caption: Three separate guesses, and a person approves the final name.

sections.heading: It gets better as you use it
body: Every document someone approves becomes a new example. When an expert chooses to retrain, it learns from the office's own decisions, and if an approval gets undone, that example comes back out.

media.alt: Feedback-loop diagram showing an approved document becoming a labeled example, deliberate expert retraining, updated cues and similarity, and removal if the approval is later reversed
media.caption: Approved documents teach it, and undone ones get taken back out.

sections.heading: Built for the team
body: One paper packet could show up as several scans, and big plan sheets were scanned separately and added later. So I added a staging screen to put the pieces in order, rotate them and merge them before processing. I also added accounts, roles and a second check, so helpers could do a first pass and an expert could sign off. A lot of this came from talking with the people doing the scanning and filing.

media.alt: Scan staging workspace showing separate document parts, a multi-page preview, and controls for combining the pages
media.caption: Putting separate scans in order before merging them.

media.alt: Signal Scanner dashboard actively processing a folder while hundreds of completed documents wait in the review queue
media.caption: A big batch processing while finished documents wait for review.

sections.heading: How well it worked
body: When it was confident enough to suggest filing, it matched the county's existing category about 97% of the time, and in a blind test it got the type right on all 26 documents. Dates and exact file names were much harder, which is why a person still checks every one.
I built it fast with a lot of help from AI. My job was mostly deciding what was safe to automate and testing it against real documents.

notes: SOURCES: Michael's dictated accounts on 2026-09-13, cross-checked against a read-only review of the authorized USB archive's signal_scanner project. Reviewed README.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, requirements.txt, setup documentation, and representative OCR, text normalization, cue mining, TF-IDF/kNN, LLM, fusion, extraction, naming, packet parsing, staging, page editing, auth, security, queue, review, learning, storage, and web UI source. NOT RUN: The system depends on the employer's documents, local signal lookup, Ollama model, Windows runtime, and environment configuration. No .env file, account database, OCR cache, queue/history data, production filename fixtures, stored documents, or other workplace records were opened during source review. TERMINOLOGY: Michael called one OCR component 'Docstring'; the source uses Docling plus RapidOCR. EMBEDDING CLARIFICATION: Michael recalled training an embedding text model from about 146 categorized documents. The preserved system builds a labeled corpus of 141 already-filed documents and implements optional Ollama embeddings, but its measured configuration disables embeddings because embeddinggemma and nomic-embed-text did not improve leave-one-out accuracy. Visible copy therefore describes the tested embedding work but identifies character/word TF-IDF plus mined cue phrases and the local LLM as the active three-way classifier. LEARNING LOOP: Source confirms that approvals are appended to learned.jsonl by content hash; flagged and skipped records are excluded; retraining is a deliberate action that merges the learned and base corpora, re-mines cues, and refits the classifier; undo, reopen, and purge paths remove learned entries so corrected mistakes do not persist. OCR/HANDWRITING: Michael observed successful handwriting recognition in some scans. Source evaluation also records that handwritten dates were missing from OCR on a meaningful subset, so visible copy says some handwriting was recovered but not consistently. MODEL: Architecture documentation identifies Ollama qwen3.5:4b, schema-constrained output, temperature 0, and efficient mode that skips the LLM when the other two voters agree. SCALE: The 50 cabinets, approximately 300,000 pages, and records dating to 1972 come from Michael's direct account. Source documentation separately describes approximately 40,000 scanned documents, roughly 140 labeled examples, and more than 2,000 signals; pages and documents are not treated as equivalent. EVALUATION: Visible percentages are rounded from the preserved measurements: 80.9% overall and 97.1% above confidence 0.60 without the LLM; 26 of 26 category-correct in the small blind full-pipeline test. The same test had substantially weaker date and exact-name accuracy, which is stated to avoid presenting type accuracy as end-to-end accuracy. DEVELOPMENT DISCLOSURE: Michael explicitly classifies the implementation as AI-assisted and describes extensive AI prototyping for an internal-use prototype. OWNERSHIP/STATUS: The work summary calls the initial signal_scanner repository a sole-author document OCR prototype. The archive contains a much more extensive uncommitted working tree beyond the two recorded prototype commits. Visible copy describes Michael's ownership of the prototype without calling it a deployed production system. TEAM INPUT: The section about talking with scanning staff, reviewers, and programming/data teammates comes from Michael's direct account. Specific workflow details attributed to those conversations are also reflected in source comments and UI behavior, but individual people and employer details are omitted. NETWORK CLARIFICATION: Source supports local execution shared over the office network, not public internet hosting. SECURITY: Public copy summarizes roles, sessions, magic links, audit history, and locking but omits internal addresses, filenames, paths, keys, and configuration. PUBLIC-SAFETY EDITS: Client and employer names, internal application acronym, exact folder layout, and database schema details are omitted or generalized. MEDIA/LINKS: Four screenshots supplied by Michael on 2026-09-15 were added to the page. The two dashboard captures were cropped only to remove browser chrome; the application content was not recreated or altered. The screenshots show representative queue, review, and staging states selected by Michael for public portfolio use. No public repository or demo was verified. No third-party logos or generic internet images were added. The three diagrams were written in Mermaid from the documented architecture, rendered locally, converted to WebP through the portfolio media pipeline, and contain no internal data. The manual-workflow comparison uses Michael's description of File Explorer, a PDF viewer, renaming, and spreadsheet tracking. DATE: 2026-07 is supported by the repository's two recorded commits and the internship work summary; later uncommitted development exists, but its exact dates are not verified.
